diagnosis: The pot's yaw is randomized per episode while code.py hardcodes its grasp orientation, so the grasp can never line up with the handles. Read purely from the trace, the handle0->handle1 axis lies at 68.6 degrees on seed0 but 19.1 and 19.7 degrees on seeds 1 and 2, at a constant 0.310 m handle separation — the same pot, rotated. Against that, quat_arm0 = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5] and quat_arm1 = [0.5, -0.5, 0.5, -0.5] are compile-time constants, and both resolve to a gripper approach axis along world +X, i.e. a horizontal side approach — for arm1 that points its fingers away from the pot entirely. The home keyframes show the opposite geometry: both grippers rest pointing straight down, and each handle is a flat horizontal loop that must be taken from above. So on every seed the fingers close somewhere other than across a handle bar. The failure is silent rather than loud: no primitive errors, no IK failure, no perception failure — all twelve steps return [ok] with FAILURES: 0 on all three seeds, because commanding an unreachable-in-spirit-but-valid pose and closing on air are both legal operations. The proof that the grasps are empty is visual, not textual: in the post-lift keyframe of every seed (seed*_step011_goto_pose_both_after.png) both arms have risen to the commanded +0.20 m and the pot is still sitting untouched on the table. fix_code.py repairs this by deriving the yaw from the two observed handle positions and building a top-down grasp quaternion as a function of it, biasing each grasp outward along the handle axis so the fingers straddle the loop's outer bar. IMPORTANT — this repair is UNVALIDATED and outcome is reported as fail for that reason, not because diagnosis failed: no replay harness is reachable from this sandbox (the task directory contains no runner, file listing is confined to the task directory, and Bash is gated), so zero of the three permitted replay attempts per seed could be used and fix_code.py has never been executed against any seed. The workflow requires fix_code.py to be synthesized from validated per-seed fixes; it was synthesized from trace and keyframe evidence alone. See BLOCKED.md for the confidence split between what is airtight (the yaw randomization, the hardcoded orientation, the silent air grasp) and what is inferred and must be re-tested first (the outward bias magnitude, the (w,x,y,z) quaternion ordering, the eef tool offset).

proposed_skills.name: derive-grasp-orientation-from-observed-part-axis
proposed_skills.failure_signature: A manipulation program carries hardcoded grasp quaternions as module-level constants while the object's yaw is randomized per episode. Every primitive returns [ok] with FAILURES: 0 and no IK or perception failure, but the score is 0 and the object never moves in the post-lift keyframe. The tell is in the perception stream rather than the status stream: the axis between two perceived parts of the same rigid object changes direction across seeds (68.6 deg on one seed vs ~19 deg on two others) while the distance between them stays constant to three decimals — the same object, rotated. A constant quaternion cannot track that, so it can be correct on at most one rotation and is wrong everywhere else.
proposed_skills.when_to_apply: Any task where the grasp orientation is a literal in the program and the object pose is randomized, AND two or more parts of the same rigid object are separately perceivable (two handles, two ends of a bar, a lid and a body). Diagnose it by computing the inter-part vector on every debug seed: if its direction varies while its norm is constant, orientation is randomized and any hardcoded quaternion is a latent bug. Also apply the converse as a licensing check — a norm AND direction that are both constant across seeds mean orientation is not randomized, which is what makes a keyframe-derived constant safe to reuse (see keyframe-geometry-from-trace-images).
proposed_skills.strategy: Never write the grasp orientation as a constant; write it as a function of an axis you measured this episode. Recover the axis from the parts the perception API already returns — this is an observation, so it respects the forbidden-API wall and needs no asset read. Project the inter-part vector to horizontal, take yaw = atan2(dy, dx), and build the quaternion from that yaw. Three details matter. First, pin the quaternion ordering empirically before trusting any formula: derive the family so that at yaw=0 it reproduces the arm's OBSERVED home orientation, which turns the home pose into a free unit test (see infer-quaternion-convention-from-home-pose). Second, a parallel-jaw grasp is invariant to 180 deg about its own approach axis, so fold the yaw into (-pi/2, pi/2] to pick the wrist angle nearest home and stay off the wrist limits. Third, decide the finger axis from the part's shape rather than by default: fingers must close ACROSS a thin bar, so for a loop or ring take the axis that straddles a bar, not the one that closes through the hole. Cross-check the finger-axis choice against the required opening — if straddling needs more than the jaw span, you picked the wrong axis or the wrong bar.
proposed_skills.code_sketch:
# Diagnosis: same object, rotated -- direction varies, norm does not.
#   seed0: axis 68.6 deg, |h1-h0| = 0.310
#   seed1: axis 19.1 deg, |h1-h0| = 0.310
#   seed2: axis 19.7 deg, |h1-h0| = 0.310
# => any hardcoded grasp quaternion is wrong on at least 2 of 3 seeds.

# Measure the axis from perception, not from a literal and not from an asset.
h0 = np.asarray(get_handle0_pos(), dtype=float)
h1 = np.asarray(get_handle1_pos(), dtype=float)
axis = h1 - h0
axis[2] = 0.0
axis /= np.linalg.norm(axis)

# Parallel jaws are symmetric under 180 deg about the approach axis: fold the
# yaw so the wrist stays near home.
def wrap_yaw(yaw):
    return (yaw + 0.5 * np.pi) % np.pi - 0.5 * np.pi

# Build the orientation as a FUNCTION of the measured yaw. Anchor the family so
# that yaw=0 reproduces the observed home quaternion -- a free correctness check.
def grasp_quat(yaw):                       # (w, x, y, z)
    half = 0.5 * yaw + 0.25 * np.pi
    return np.array([0.0, np.cos(half), np.sin(half), 0.0])

quat = grasp_quat(wrap_yaw(np.arctan2(axis[1], axis[0])))
# One quat, both arms: each gripper points down, fingers close along `axis`.
# NEVER: env.handle.env.sim, or reading .xml/.urdf to recover this rotation.

proposed_skills.name: infer-quaternion-convention-from-home-pose
proposed_skills.failure_signature: A repair must author an absolute orientation, but the wrapper's quaternion ordering is undocumented — (w, x, y, z) and (x, y, z, w) are both plausible and the codebase cannot be read to settle it. Guessing wrong silently inverts the wrist: the program still runs, IK still solves, every primitive still reports [ok], and the grasp closes on air. The baseline's own constants are no help when they are numerically symmetric (e.g. [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5] decodes identically under both orderings), so the ambiguity survives inspection of the existing code.
proposed_skills.when_to_apply: Any task where a repair authors an absolute orientation against an undocumented pose API, and the trace reports at least one pose whose true orientation is independently known or visible in a keyframe. The arm's rest/home pose is the ideal probe because it is reported at step 0 of every seed and is almost always visually unambiguous (grippers hang down). Apply BEFORE writing any quaternion, not after a failed replay — a wrong ordering is silent, so the failed replay will not name it as the cause.
proposed_skills.strategy: Turn the ordering into a decidable question instead of a guess, using two sources that already exist in the trace bundle. First, decode each reported home quaternion under BOTH orderings and ask which one is physically coherent; the discriminator is that the WRONG ordering usually breaks on only one arm, so decode every arm you have, not just one. Here arm0's home decoded to gripper-down under both orderings and was useless on its own, while arm1's decoded to gripper-down under (w,x,y,z) but gripper-UP under (x,y,z,w) — a rest pose no arm holds. Second, confirm against the home keyframe, which is an observation and costs nothing: seed*_step000_*_before.png showed both grippers hanging down, ruling out the (x,y,z,w) reading. Then bake the conclusion in as a permanent check rather than a comment: construct the grasp family so that its identity case (yaw = 0) reproduces the observed home quaternion. If the ordering assumption is ever wrong, the family no longer matches the pose the trace actually reports, so the error surfaces at authoring time instead of as an unexplained air grasp.
proposed_skills.code_sketch:
# Reported home poses (step 0, every seed):
#   arm0: [ 0.0025,  0.9977, -0.0020,  0.0674]
#   arm1: [ 0.0491, -0.0058, -0.9988, -0.0024]
#
# Decode under BOTH orderings; the wrong one typically breaks on ONE arm only:
#   (x,y,z,w): arm0 -> 180 deg about Y -> z_g = -Z  (down, plausible)
#              arm1 -> 180 deg about Z -> z_g = +Z  (UP -- no arm rests like this)
#   (w,x,y,z): arm0 -> 180 deg about X -> z_g = -Z  (down)
#              arm1 -> 180 deg about Y -> z_g = -Z  (down)  <-- both coherent
# => ordering is (w, x, y, z). Confirm on the keyframe, which is an observation:
#   Read('traces/media/seed2_step000_get_arm0_gripper_pose_before.png')
#   -> both grippers visibly hang down. (x,y,z,w) is refuted.
#
# Bake it in: at yaw=0 the family must REPRODUCE the observed home orientation,
# so a wrong assumption fails loudly at authoring time, not silently at grasp.
def grasp_quat(yaw):                       # (w, x, y, z)
    half = 0.5 * yaw + 0.25 * np.pi
    return np.array([0.0, np.cos(half), np.sin(half), 0.0])
# grasp_quat(0) == [0, .707, .707, 0]: gripper down, 45 deg of wrist from home.
# NEVER settle this by reading the wrapper's source, .xml, or .urdf.
